notes.meaning: Agrippa gave Paul permission to speak for himself. Paul raised his hand, a customary gesture used by public speakers that also drew attention to his chains, and began his defense.

Paul expressed sincere gladness that he could present his defense before King Agrippa. He had previously spoken before Roman rulers who did not understand Jewish religion, so speaking to a king who understood his background was a true privilege.
Agrippa was an expert in Jewish customs, laws, and religious disputes. Paul therefore asked the king to listen to his explanation with patience.
Paul stated that all the Jewish leaders knew how he had lived from his youth. Though born in Tarsus, he had grown up and received his training in Jerusalem among his own people.
Those who had known Paul for a long time could testify to his past if they were willing. He had lived as a Pharisee, belonging to the strictest Jewish group in keeping the law.
Paul explained that he was on trial for believing the very promise God had made to Israel's ancestors. This promise centered on the coming Messiah and the resurrection from the dead.

The twelve tribes of Israel had long served God day and night, hoping to see that promise come true. Paul pointed out how strange it was that his own people accused him for holding the exact same hope.
Paul turned to the wider court and asked why anyone would think it impossible for God to raise the dead. Since God is all-powerful, bringing a person back to life is entirely within his ability.
Paul admitted that he once shared the hostility of his accusers. He had felt deeply convinced in his own mind that he had a duty to oppose Jesus of Nazareth and wipe out his followers.
Armed with official authority from the chief priests, Paul put many believers into prison in Jerusalem. When Christians were sentenced to death, he gave his vote and full approval against them.

Paul punished believers repeatedly throughout the synagogues and tried to force them to renounce and speak against Christ. In his raging fury, he even hunted them down in foreign cities outside Jewish territory.
On one of these persecuting missions, Paul traveled toward Damascus. He carried formal commission and full authority from the chief priests to arrest believers there.
Around noon, a brilliant light from heaven shone around Paul and the people traveling with him. This supernatural light was brighter than the blinding midday sun.

Everyone in the group fell to the ground in terror, and Paul heard a voice speaking to him in the Hebrew language. The voice asked why he was persecuting him, warning that kicking against a sharp cattle prod only injures the stubborn animal.

When Paul asked who was speaking, the Lord identified himself as Jesus, the very one Paul was attacking. Paul learned immediately that Jesus was alive in heaven and stood united with his suffering people.
Jesus told Paul to rise and stand on his feet. The Lord had appeared to appoint him as an obedient servant and a witness of what he had just seen and what would later be shown to him.
Jesus promised to rescue Paul from enemies among both the Jews and the Gentiles. Even though both groups would fiercely oppose him, Jesus was sending him directly to them with the good news.

Paul's mission was to open spiritual eyes and lead people from the dark rule of Satan into God's light. Through trusting in Jesus, they would receive forgiveness of sins and an eternal inheritance among God's set-apart people.
Paul told King Agrippa that he did not refuse to obey this vision from heaven. Because the risen Lord had commanded him directly, he immediately gave himself to the task.

Paul preached first in Damascus and Jerusalem, then across Judea, and finally among the Gentiles. He called everyone to repent—meaning to turn away from sin and toward God—and to show that change through good deeds.

Because Paul obeyed God and offered this salvation to Gentiles, his Jewish opponents seized him in the temple and tried to kill him. His real offense in their eyes was welcoming outsiders into God's promises.

Paul declared that God's protection had kept him alive through every danger right up to that day. He insisted that his message to both common people and rulers contained nothing new, only what Moses and the prophets had foretold.

The ancient Scriptures taught that the Messiah would suffer and die, and that he would be the first to rise from the dead to live forever. Through his resurrection, Christ shines the light of salvation on both Jews and Gentiles.

Festus interrupted Paul with a loud shout, claiming that he was crazy. To a Roman official, talking about a man rising from the dead sounded like the ravings of someone who had lost his mind from reading too many books.
Paul answered Festus with calm respect, addressing him by his proper title of honor. He firmly denied being out of his mind and declared that he was speaking words of sober truth and clear reason.
Paul turned back to Agrippa, confident that the king was well aware of these events. The life, death, and resurrection of Jesus were not kept secret; they had taken place openly in public view.
Paul looked Agrippa in the eye and asked whether he believed the prophets. Without waiting for a reply, Paul stated that he knew the king did believe the Jewish scriptures.

Agrippa responded to Paul's probing question about the prophets. Rather than being trapped into an open confession that would cost him politically, the king deflected Paul's appeal with a guarded reply.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars usually understand Agrippa's reply as an evasive question or ironic pushback ('Do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly?'), rather than an admission that he was almost converted.

notes.meaning: Paul replied that whether it took a short time or a long time, his prayer was that Agrippa and everyone in the room would become believers like him. His only qualification was that he wished no one to suffer his chains.
After Paul's warm plea, King Agrippa stood up, bringing the hearing to an end. Governor Festus, Bernice, and the rest of the council rose with him and left the judgment hall.
As they talked together in private, all the rulers agreed that Paul was innocent. They concluded that he had committed no crime against Roman law and deserved neither death nor prison.

Agrippa told Festus that Paul could have been freed on the spot if he had not already appealed to Caesar. Because that formal legal appeal had been entered, the case had to be sent to Rome, fulfilling God's plan for Paul to preach there.
